claims.text: Increasing the density of undercoordinated surface sites on platinum-group metal nanoparticles will increase ethanol-oxidation activity.
Increasing the density of undercoordinated surface sites will increase selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Undercoordinated sites stabilize reactive oxygenated intermediates.
Stabilization of reactive oxygenated intermediates facilitates a direct 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Low-temperature hydrogen plasma treatment can selectively etch platinum-group metal nanoparticle surfaces and create additional surface defects.
Hydrogen plasma treatment will increase the density of undercoordinated atoms and lattice defects at the nanoparticle surface.
Defective surface sites lower the energy barrier for ethanol adsorption.
Defective surface sites lower the energy barrier for subsequent ethanol dehydrogenation steps.
Intermediate stabilization at defective sites promotes complete oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
Complete oxidation of ethanol to CO2 is a 12-electron process.
Defective sites reduce the formation of poisoning intermediates and thereby improve catalyst durability.
Hydrogen plasma-treated catalysts will have higher peak current densities than untreated, thermally reduced catalysts.
Hydrogen plasma-treated catalysts will have a larger turnover frequency than untreated catalysts.
Hydrogen plasma-treated catalysts will produce a higher CO2-to-acetaldehyde/acetic-acid ratio than untreated catalysts.
The beneficial effect of plasma-created defects is expected below approximately 0.8 V versus RHE, where the surface remains sufficiently reduced.
Above approximately 0.8 V versus RHE, excessive surface-oxide formation may mask the beneficial effects of defects.
Nanoparticle size and metal-support interactions may alter the observable effect of defect engineering.
